screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday on the Pandavas' last journey, the twins fell: Sahadeva for thinking no one his equal in wisdom, Nakula in beauty. Did you catch a comparison and drop it? Day eight hundred seventy-six.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY.` · `THE TWINS FALL.`

segments.voice: Arjuna, who threw his bow into the sea, is still walking. He's the one who heard the Gita in the chariot, who won Draupadi at her bridegroom-choice, who fought through the war. Then, on the high road, grief at his brothers' falling seems to catch up with him, and Arjuna falls too. Bhima, who has asked why each time, asks again. And a little later, Bhima the strong feels his own legs go. Lying on the ground, Bhima calls out one more question, this time about himself. Today, the last two brothers fall.
screen: `ARJUNA STILL WALKING.` → `ARJUNA FALLS.` → `BHIMA ASKS ABOUT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: About Arjuna, Yudhishthira's answer in Ganguli's telling has two parts. Arjuna once said he would destroy all their enemies in a single day, and he didn't do it. And he looked down on other bowmen. A boast that went unkept, and a habit of disregard. Then Bhima falls, and he doesn't ask about anyone else this time. He calls out: I'm falling too. Why? And Yudhishthira answers him directly. You ate too much, he says, and you boasted of your strength, and you ate without a thought for what others needed. Then he walks on. Now look back down this whole road. Draupadi, the twins, Arjuna, Bhima. Each fall comes with a reason, and each reason is small and specific: a heart that leaned, a comparison, a boast, an appetite. Not one of them is a great crime. These are people who did great things and, in this telling, carried one ordinary weight too many up a mountain. One more detail. Bhima, who asked every time, the brother who kept stopping to look, is the last to fall before Yudhishthira is alone. The question why goes with him. The text leaves no verdict on the verdicts, only an image: one man, still walking, toward the top of the world. And behind him, the only one left, not a brother, not a queen, the dog.
screen: `ARJUNA: AN UNKEPT BOAST` · `BHIMA: "WHY AM I FALLING?"` · `EACH REASON SMALL AND SPECIFIC` · then, large: `ONE MAN WALKING, AND A DOG`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath settle low in your body. Ask yourself Bhima's question, gently: what's one ordinary weight I'm carrying that I don't need? An old boast, a grudge, a habit of too much. Don't make a list. Just let one come. Breathe in and name it. Breathe out and imagine setting it down on the path. Then sit with the lighter feeling, without hurrying on. If you pray, you can offer that weight in your prayer. The bell holds the time.

877.howItsDone: The story of Yudhishthira and the dog comes from the Mahaprasthanika Parva of the Mahabharata; Hindus hear it in recitations and retellings of the epic, and some retellers draw from it a lesson in loyalty and dharma.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday on the Pandavas' last journey, Arjuna fell, then Bhima, and Yudhishthira walked on with only the dog. Did you set down one small weight? Day eight hundred seventy-seven.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY.` · `ONE BY ONE THEY FALL.`

segments.voice: Two of them are left on the mountain: a king and a dog. Yudhishthira's brothers have fallen behind him. Draupadi has fallen. The dog that joined them at the start of the road has not. It is still at his heel. Then the sky fills with sound, and Indra, king of the gods, pulls up in a chariot and tells Yudhishthira to climb in. Heaven is waiting. This is the moment the whole road has been leading to. And in Ganguli's telling, Yudhishthira's first answer is not yes. It's a question about who gets to come with him.
screen: `A KING AND A DOG.` → `INDRA'S CHARIOT ARRIVES.` → `"CLIMB IN."`

segments.voice: First he asks about his brothers and Draupadi. He won't go without them. Indra reassures him: they are already in heaven. They left their bodies on the way. You, he says, will go up in yours. So far, good news. Then Yudhishthira says the dog has been devoted to him, and it should come too. And Indra says no. You have won heaven and a state like a god's, he says. Leave the dog. There is no cruelty in that. Heaven has no place for people with dogs. Notice how reasonable it sounds. It's only a dog. The offer is enormous. And there is no one to speak for the dog but him. Yudhishthira refuses. In the text he says that turning away one who is devoted to you, who is frightened and has nowhere else to go, is a grave wrong, and that he will not give it up even for his own happiness. Heaven or no heaven, the dog stays with him. Then the dog changes. It is Dharma, the god of righteousness, Yudhishthira's own father, who has been walking beside him in disguise. Dharma praises him. He reminds his son of an earlier test, in the forest, at a lake, when Yudhishthira was asked to choose one brother to bring back to life and chose Nakula, the son of his other mother, out of fairness. Now he has chosen again, for a dog. Only then does Yudhishthira climb into the chariot. The epic was long and full of wars. This examination turns out to be very small: whether a king will keep faith with a creature that can't repay him.
screen: `"NOT WITHOUT MY BROTHERS"` · `INDRA: LEAVE THE DOG` · `"I WILL NOT TURN IT AWAY"` · then, large: `THE DOG IS DHARMA`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind a creature or a person who depends on you and can't give much back. A pet. A small child. A parent who needs more help now. Breathe in and simply see them near you. Breathe out and let your shoulders soften. You don't have to promise anything. Just notice that they're still there. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer for a moment. The bell holds the time.

878.title: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
878.hook: Yudhishthira reaches heaven and finds his old enemy enthroned there, and his brothers nowhere in sight
878.carry: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
878.howItsDone: The Svargarohana Parva is the last book of the Mahabharata; Hindus hear its ending in recitations of the full epic, and some retellings of the epic linger on Yudhishthira's choice to stay with his family.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Pandavas' last journey reached Indra's chariot, and Yudhishthira would not leave the dog, who turned out to be Dharma. Did you do a small kindness for someone who stuck with you? Day eight hundred seventy-eight.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA'S DOG.` · `THE DOG IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: The chariot sets him down in heaven, and the first face Yudhishthira sees is Duryodhana's. The cousin behind the rigged game of dice. The man who had Draupadi dragged into the hall. The one who would not make peace. He is sitting in splendor, honored among the gods. Yudhishthira's brothers are nowhere. Draupadi is nowhere. Karna is nowhere. And the man who refused heaven's chariot rather than abandon a dog now says, in effect, that he does not want this heaven. Take me to my brothers, he says. Wherever they are, that's where I want to be.
screen: `DURYODHANA, ENTHRONED.` → `NO BROTHERS. NO DRAUPADI.` → `"TAKE ME TO THEM."`

segments.voice: The sage Narada tries to calm him. This is heaven, he says; old quarrels end here. Duryodhana died fighting as a warrior, and this is where that leads. Yudhishthira won't be calmed. So the gods send a messenger to guide him to his family. The path turns dark. It smells of decay. There are thorns, burning things, bodies, a river that scalds. It is a hell. Yudhishthira has had enough, and turns to go back. And then voices call out of the dark. Stay, they beg him. While you stand here, a cool breeze blows and our pain eases. He asks who they are. Karna, they answer. Bhima. Arjuna. Nakula. Sahadeva. Dhrishtadyumna. Draupadi. The sons of Draupadi. Everyone he loved is here, in torment, while the man who caused the war sits on a throne. Yudhishthira is furious, at the gods and at dharma itself. And then he makes his choice. He tells the messenger to go back without him. If his presence comforts them, he will stay in hell. That is the moment it ends. Indra and the gods appear. The darkness lifts. It was an illusion, Indra explains; every king must glimpse hell, and Yudhishthira saw it because of his own deception in the war, about Drona's son. Dharma says his son has been tested once more and has held. Then Yudhishthira bathes in the heavenly Ganga, leaves his human body, and finds his brothers and Draupadi in their own true forms. The serial that began with a family quarrel ends with a man who would rather share his family's pain than enjoy a heaven without them.
screen: `NARADA: OLD QUARRELS END HERE` · `VOICES IN THE DARK: "STAY"` · `HE CHOOSES TO STAY IN HELL` · then, large: `THE ILLUSION LIFTS`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest. This is the end of a very long story, so give it a quiet minute. Breathe in, and bring to mind one person whose hard time you would rather share than be spared from. Breathe out, and let the wish to fix it loosen a little. Just stand near them in your mind, the way Yudhishthira stood in the dark. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If not, just keep them company. The bell holds the time.

879.title: the birth
879.hook: a wedding procession, a brother driving the bride's chariot, and a voice from the sky that turns him into a killer
879.howItsDone: The story of Krishna's birth is told in the tenth book of the Bhagavata Purana; Hindus hear it in recitations and festival retellings, especially around Krishna Janmashtami.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Pandavas' last journey ended in heaven, after Yudhishthira chose to stand in the dark beside his family. That closes the Mahabharata serial. Today a new book opens, the Bhagavata Purana, and a new story: Krishna as a child. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY ENDS.` · `A NEW BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: The wedding is over and the music is still playing. Devaki, a princess of the Yadu clan, has just married Vasudeva, and they are riding home together. Her cousin Kamsa, a prince of Mathura, wants to honor her, so he takes the reins himself and drives the bridal chariot. Conches, drums, gifts of horses and elephants. A happy brother on a happy day. And then, the Bhagavata says, a voice speaks out of the sky, without a body, straight at the driver. Fool, it says. The eighth child of the woman you are driving will kill you.
screen: `A WEDDING CHARIOT.` → `KAMSA HOLDS THE REINS.` → `A VOICE FROM THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Kamsa's answer is instant. He grabs his cousin by the hair and draws his sword. The wedding procession stops dead. What happens next is the first surprise of this story. Vasudeva doesn't fight. He talks. In the Bhagavata he reasons with Kamsa, gently. Death, he says, comes to everyone who is born, today or in a hundred years; killing a woman, your own sister, on her wedding day, won't change that. It will only stain you. Kamsa won't listen. So Vasudeva thinks fast, and he makes a terrible bargain to save his wife's life right now. I'll bring you every son she bears, he promises. They're the danger, not her. Kamsa knows Vasudeva keeps his word. He lowers the sword. And Vasudeva does keep it. When their first son is born, he carries the baby to Kamsa himself. The text praises him for this: a man who holds to truth even when it costs everything. Kamsa, for a moment, is moved. Only the eighth child is my danger, he says; take this one home. That moment of mercy doesn't last. The sage Narada visits Kamsa and stirs up his fear, and Kamsa locks Devaki and Vasudeva in a prison and begins to kill their children. This is how the story of Krishna's birth begins: not with a cradle, but with a promise made at sword point, and a father who keeps it. The book that will be full of a child's laughter starts in a prison cell.
screen: `THE SWORD COMES OUT` · `VASUDEVA REASONS WITH KAMSA` · `"I'LL BRING YOU EVERY SON"` · then, large: `A PROMISE KEPT, A PRISON CELL`

You don't need the right words yet. Just practice the steadiness. If you pray, you can ask in your own way for a calm voice. The bell holds the time.
The birth. Krishna's story starts before he is born, with a voice at a wedding and a promise Vasudeva keeps.

880.title: the birth
880.hook: in Kamsa's prison, a child is quietly moved from one mother to another, and the gods come to sing to an unborn baby
880.howItsDone: The prayer the gods offer to the child in Devaki's womb, told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book, is heard when the Bhagavata is recited, and Balarama is honored alongside Krishna in temples and festivals.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the birth began at a wedding: a voice from the sky, Kamsa's sword, and Vasudeva's promise, kept. Did a calm word help anywhere yesterday? Day eight hundred eighty.
screen: `THE WEDDING CHARIOT.` · `A PROMISE KEPT.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata doesn't linger on it, and neither will we. In the prison, Kamsa kills Devaki's children as they are born. The text says that when six had died, a seventh child began to grow in her. And this time, something is done in secret. The Lord, the Bhagavata says, calls on his own power of illusion, Yogamaya, and gives her a task. A child is in danger. Move him. Today, the hidden work that happens before the birth.
screen: `A PRISON IN MATHURA.` → `THE SEVENTH CHILD.` → `"MOVE HIM."`

segments.voice: Yogamaya draws the seventh child out of Devaki's womb and places him in the womb of Rohini, another wife of Vasudeva, who is living safely in Gokula, a village of cowherds across the river. In the prison, people say Devaki has miscarried. In Gokula, the child grows in secret. The Bhagavata names him from that night: he will be called Sankarshana, the one who was drawn out. Later he is known as Balarama, Krishna's older brother. So the first rescue in this story is quiet and invisible. Then the Lord himself enters Devaki. The text says he first enters Vasudeva's mind, and from there passes into Devaki, and she begins to shine. The prison can't hold the light. Kamsa sees her glowing and understands: this is the one. But he can't bring himself to kill a pregnant woman, his own cousin, and so he waits, and the waiting turns into obsession. The Bhagavata says that sitting, lying down, eating, walking, Kamsa saw that child everywhere. His fear made him think of the Lord constantly. And while Kamsa paces, the gods come. Brahma, Shiva and the others arrive and stand in the cell to sing praise to the child inside Devaki. Do not be afraid, mother, they tell her. The one in your womb has come to protect the world. It's a strange and tender scene: a dark cell, a frightened mother, a jailer outside, and inside it the whole sky gathered around someone who hasn't been born yet.
screen: `THE SEVENTH CHILD IS MOVED` · `SANKARSHANA: DRAWN OUT` · `KAMSA SEES HIM EVERYWHERE` · then, large: `THE GODS SING TO THE UNBORN CHILD`

Breathe in, and let yourself notice it, without hurrying it. Breathe out, and let go of the urge to check on it. The gods in the story came just to stand near something that hadn't arrived. You can do the same. If you pray, you can hold it in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The birth. Before it happens, a brother is moved to safety, a mother begins to shine, and the gods come to sing.

881.title: the birth
881.hook: at midnight in a dark prison, a child appears with four arms, and his mother asks him to look like an ordinary baby
881.howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Krishna's birth at Janmashtami, and in homes and temples some devotees keep watch until midnight, the hour the Bhagavata gives for the birth, and then celebrate.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, before the birth: Balarama moved in secret to Rohini, Devaki shining in the prison, the gods singing to a child not yet born. What good thing did you leave alone to grow? Day eight hundred eighty-one.
screen: `SANKARSHANA, DRAWN OUT.` · `THE GODS SING.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata sets the scene slowly, as if it doesn't want to rush the night. The sky is clear. The rivers run clean. Lotuses open on the lakes, and birds and bees fill the woods with sound. A cool, fragrant breeze moves. The sacred fires of the brahmanas burn bright and steady. And in the middle of the night, in deep darkness, inside a locked cell in Mathura, the text says the Lord appeared from Devaki the way the full moon rises in the east. Today, the moment the whole story has been waiting for.
screen: `A CLEAR SKY, CLEAN RIVERS.` → `MIDNIGHT, DEEP DARKNESS.` → `LIKE THE FULL MOON RISING.`

segments.voice: Vasudeva looks at the newborn, and it is not an ordinary baby. The child has four arms, holding a conch, a mace, a discus and a lotus. A jewel shines at his throat. He wears yellow silk. Vasudeva knows exactly who this is. He folds his hands and praises him: you are the one beyond all things, and you have come into this house. Then Devaki speaks. Her praise is lovely, and then it turns very practical, very much a mother's. Please, she says, hide this form. Kamsa must not know you have been born here. And this shape, with the conch and discus, is too much for ordinary eyes. Become small. The Lord answers by telling them a secret. He has been their child before. In an earlier age, he says, they spent long years in austerity, asking for a son like him, and he was born to them. Then again in another life. Now this is the third time. Remember me as your son, he tells them, and you will reach me. And then, while they watch, he does what his mother asked. The four arms, the jewel, the radiance: gone. On the prison floor there is a newborn, like any other. That is the heart of the birth in this telling. The Lord of the universe arrives at full height, and the first thing he does, at his mother's request, is make himself small enough to be held and hidden. In this telling, the childhood stories to come, the butter, the mischief, the cowherds, grow out of that one choice.

882.title: the crossing of the Yamuna
882.hook: the guards fall asleep, the bolted doors swing open, and Vasudeva walks out into a storm carrying a newborn
882.howItsDone: The crossing of the Yamuna is retold at Janmashtami in songs, plays and temple tableaux, and the image of Vasudeva carrying the infant through the river under Shesha's hoods is a familiar one in Hindu art.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth: four arms at midnight, and then, at Devaki's request, an ordinary baby on the prison floor. What small moment did you treat as precious? Day eight hundred eighty-two, the end of a week.
screen: `MIDNIGHT IN THE PRISON.` · `HE BECOMES SMALL.`

segments.voice: The baby has only just been born, and he cannot stay. Kamsa's guards are just outside. The Bhagavata says that Vasudeva, prompted by the Lord himself, picks up his son. And then the prison starts to come undone. The guards slump into sleep. The doors, bolted and barred with iron, open on their own, the way darkness gives way to the sun. Outside, rain is falling and the clouds rumble low. Somewhere ahead, in the dark, is the river. Today Vasudeva walks out of the prison with his son.
screen: `A NEWBORN SON.` → `THE GUARDS SLEEP.` → `THE DOORS OPEN BY THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Notice who does what. The miracles open the way, but they don't carry the child. Vasudeva does that, in his own arms, through a storm, at night. The Bhagavata adds two details. First, the rain. As Vasudeva walks, Shesha, the great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, follows behind him and spreads his hoods over the father and child like an umbrella. The cosmic serpent, holding off the weather for a newborn. Then the river. The Yamuna that night is swollen and fast, the text says, full of waves and whirlpools and foam, deep enough to stop anyone. And the river makes way. The Bhagavata compares it to the ocean giving way for Rama, when he crossed to Lanka to bring back Sita. The same Lord, another age, another stretch of water opening. Later retellings add more. In some, Vasudeva carries the baby in a basket on his head; in some, the river rises to touch the child's feet before it parts. Those details belong to the retellings; the Bhagavata's own account is shorter: the father, the child, the serpent, the river giving way. Look back over this week and it has the same shape again and again. Yudhishthira refusing to leave a dog. Yudhishthira staying in the dark with his family. Vasudeva keeping a terrible promise. Now Vasudeva, walking into a flood with a baby. Help arrives in this week's stories, but someone still has to walk.
screen: `THE FATHER CARRIES THE CHILD` · `SHESHA SPREADS HIS HOODS` · `THE RIVER GIVES WAY` · then, large: `SOMEONE STILL HAS TO WALK`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your feet rest flat on the floor. Feel their weight. Vasudeva crossed on foot. Breathe in, and bring to mind something you are carrying right now for someone else, a worry, a task, a person who depends on you. Breathe out, and notice what has been holding off the rain for you: a friend, a habit, a faith, a bit of luck. Let yourself see both, the carrying and the shelter. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own way. The bell holds the time.
The crossing of the Yamuna. A father carries his newborn through a storm, under a serpent's hoods, and the river gives way.
